title: Arithmetic definability: enumerable sets and quantifiers

based_on.title: Introduction to computability theory
based_on.pages: Chapter5 UCLA course extract, Proposition5A.9 p188; full selection proof

summary: Describe enumerable relations and partial computations by arithmetic formulas, and choose witnesses effectively from nonempty enumerable fibers.
abstract: A program may accept an input only after a long search; what arithmetic description captures exactly the inputs on which that search succeeds? In the standard natural numbers, the computably enumerable sets—those whose members a program can eventually recognize—are exactly the sets whose membership can be expressed by the existence of numerical witnesses followed by a bounded arithmetic check. Every quantifier in that check ranges over an explicitly bounded finite set. Universal descriptions obtained by negation capture exactly the sets whose nonmembers can be recognized, and having both kinds of description is equivalent to decidability. The halting set therefore has an arithmetic definition without a decision procedure. Requiring a program to halt on every input gives a further quantifier pattern: each input must have its own successful computation record. This separates a finite witness for one run from a requirement covering every possible input. The same finite-certificate viewpoint also supplies a partial computable witness selector for every enumerable relation, with exactly its nonempty fibers as the domain; such a selector need not return the least numerical witness.
